title: Can Venezuela’s Push for Elections Succeed?
gist: Benigno Alarcón Deza argues that Washington's three-phase Venezuela plan after Maduro's capture (stabilization, recovery, transition) is lopsided. The economic phases run on verifiable contracts, licenses, audited funds and debt restructuring, while elections remain an undated promise. Without an electoral calendar, US leverage buys the regime time and leaves Venezuela with only a 'fragile, borrowed stability'.

insights.claim: Acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez promised at the UN General Assembly to hold elections at the 'right moment', and Trump acknowledged discussing elections in their first-ever meeting. Neither set a date, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's January three-phase plan (stabilization, recovery, transition) never included dates.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Political normalization in Venezuela remains open-ended, so the risk premium for sovereign and PDVSA-linked assets should reflect an undefined political timeline.
insights.quote: The three-phase plan Secretary of State Marco Rubio disclosed in January—stabilization, recovery, and transition—never included dates
insights.locator: The three-phase plan Secretary of State

insights.claim: The key test for US Venezuela policy is whether Washington will set an electoral timetable when doing so may conflict with its immediate economic and strategic interests.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: US economic and oil goals in Venezuela may take priority over democratization, which suggests continuity of the current regime-partnered arrangement in the near term.
insights.quote: Is Washington willing to set an electoral timetable when doing so may conflict with its most immediate economic and strategic intentions?
insights.locator: The three-phase plan Secretary of State

insights.claim: Senators Ted Cruz and Bernie Moreno have pressed for free and fair elections in Venezuela, and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee was reportedly expected to review the issue in a closed-door meeting.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Congress is an emerging source of pressure that could force an electoral timetable and change the terms for US-Venezuela business.
insights.locator: CARACAS—In a matter of days, elections

insights.claim: National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez announced four elections with the presidential vote last, and the regime's appeal to 'the timeframe established by the Constitution' points to the ordinary calendar, under which it could stay in power until 2031.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: A base case of regime continuity until 2031 is plausible, which bears on the duration of contracts and on political risk in Venezuelan oil and debt deals.
insights.quote: may well extend its reign until 2031
insights.locator: Washington acknowledges that there is no deadline

themes.theme: Asymmetric US plan: contracts for economics, promises for democracy

insights.claim: The economic phases of the US Venezuela plan run through verifiable instruments: licenses, contracts, KPMG-audited funds, an IDB loan in preparation, and a controversial $150-$200 billion debt restructuring that has yet to start in earnest.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Venezuela's $150-200 billion debt restructuring and multilateral IDB lending are concrete catalysts for distressed-debt investors, though the restructuring has not really begun.
insights.quote: a controversial $150-$200 billion debt restructuring process yet to start in earnest
insights.locator: The U.S. plan is advancing, but

insights.claim: The 'biggest oil deal in world history' in Venezuela involves North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a little-known Barbados-based oil operator owned by the controversial Venezuelan entrepreneur Alejandro Betancourt.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Venezuela's flagship oil opening is going through an obscure, controversial operator, which raises governance, counterparty and reversal risk if the politics change.
insights.quote: the “biggest oil deal in world history” involving a little-known Barbados-based oil operator, North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP)
insights.locator: The U.S. plan is advancing, but

insights.claim: What matters to Washington in Venezuela is under contract, while what matters to Venezuelans has only been promised. The transition phase runs on statements, not firm commitments.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: US commercial and oil interests are locked in, while democratic change is discretionary. A future elected government could therefore challenge contracts signed in this period.
insights.quote: What matters to Washington is under contract; what matters to Venezuelans has only been promised.
insights.locator: The third phase is being implemented

insights.claim: Almost ten months after Nicolás Maduro's capture, the US exerts extraordinary and unprecedented leverage over Venezuela that shapes the actions of both the regime and the organized opposition.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Venezuela's direction depends mainly on US policy choices, so Washington's signals are the key indicator for Venezuelan risk.
insights.quote: the U.S. continues to exert extraordinary and unprecedented leverage over Venezuela
insights.locator: Almost ten months after the capture

themes.theme: Credible commitment and negotiation as time-buying

insights.claim: Drawing on Thomas Schelling's The Strategy of Conflict, a commitment is credible only when it is visible, costly to reverse and carries automatic consequences. Washington has avoided all three in Venezuela's political phase because setting a date would force it to punish a useful partner.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Without credible commitment mechanisms, election promises should be heavily discounted. Watch for dated, penalty-backed commitments as the real signal.
insights.quote: a commitment is credible when it is visible, costly to reverse, and carries automatic consequences

insights.claim: Without an election date, time works in the Venezuelan regime's favor. The 2023 Barbados Agreement already showed how commitments without automatic costs for noncompliance end.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Precedent suggests the regime will keep pledges vague and outlast pressure, so political-transition optimism is a low-probability bet.
insights.quote: Without a date, time works in the regime’s favor.

insights.claim: The second round of US-sponsored Venezuela talks ended on September 25 with a seven-member council of jurists to review Supreme Court candidates. It is nonbinding, the decision rests with a pro-government National Assembly, and four members have already served as judges.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: The concessions so far are cosmetic and do not transfer real institutional power, so the negotiations should not be read as substantive progress.
insights.locator: The negotiating dialogue has produced some

insights.claim: The Venezuelan talks deliver low-cost items and postpone those that would transfer real power: the electoral authority, the electoral calendar, political prisoners and the return of exiles. The third round, set for mid-October, has no public agenda.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Track whether the electoral authority, the calendar or political prisoners reach the agenda. Those are the markers of real transition progress.
insights.locator: The third round, scheduled for mid-October

insights.claim: In authoritarian regimes negotiation becomes a way to buy time, and in Venezuela the tactic now also serves Washington by absorbing pressure from Congress, the diaspora and allies while the US advances its objectives.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Both the regime and Washington have an incentive to prolong talks without resolution, so expect a long status quo rather than a quick transition.
insights.quote: negotiation becomes an instrument for buying time. What is new is that the tactic also serves the actor overseeing the current process.
insights.locator: The third round, scheduled for mid-October

insights.claim: Making Venezuelan elections conditional on governance, debt sustainability, state capacity and reconstruction after devastating twin earthquakes, which could take decades, amounts to postponing them indefinitely.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Reconstruction and debt workouts measured in decades imply a very long horizon for full political normalization.
insights.quote: Tying elections to the latter means postponing them indefinitely.
insights.locator: The U.S. strategy of building state

insights.claim: Following Thomas Carothers' 2007 'sequencing fallacy' critique, autocrats do not build the rule of law that would constrain them. An elected Venezuelan government would be better placed to build those conditions and ask citizens for sacrifices.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Investors betting on institutional improvement before elections may be disappointed. Durable rule-of-law gains, and contract security with them, likely require an elected government.
insights.quote: Autocrats do not build the rule of law that would constrain them.
insights.locator: The U.S. strategy of building state

themes.theme: Machado and what could shift the calculus

insights.claim: Opposition leader María Corina Machado has failed in seven attempts to return to Venezuela, amid US reluctance to facilitate her comeback. Her return would turn an administered sequence into a contest over the electoral calendar.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Machado's return is a key binary risk. It would threaten the stabilization Washington protects and could upset current oil and business arrangements, but it is essential for a credible transition.
insights.quote: For stabilization, Machado may be a risk; for a credible democratic transition, her participation is essential.
insights.locator: Machado’s eventual return to Venezuela would

insights.claim: The Venezuelan regime will democratize only when the cost of resisting exceeds the cost of yielding. Washington has lowered the cost of tolerating the regime (recognition, engagement, freedom from prosecution) without raising the cost of resisting.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Under current incentives the regime has no reason to move toward elections, so the status quo is the base case.
insights.quote: It has delivered the carrot of survival without the stick of an electoral timetable.
insights.locator: The current regime will not democratize

insights.claim: Three forces could push the Venezuelan regime toward elections: external debt restructuring, which typically makes institutional restoration a precondition for financing; US Congressional pressure for an electoral calendar; and Machado's return.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: Debt-restructuring terms are a potential lever. Creditor and multilateral conditionality could become the mechanism that ties financing to a political transition.
insights.locator: Three forces could change that calculation

insights.claim: Until there is a calendar with dates, Venezuela has only a fragile, borrowed stability, and every loan comes with a due date.
insights.speaker: BENIGNO ALARCÓN DEZA
insights.so_what: The current stability is temporary and may unwind, a tail risk for investors pricing Venezuelan oil and debt deals as durable.
insights.quote: the country only has a fragile, borrowed stability—and every loan comes with a due date
